script.opening: “Hi. So I had the bloods and stuff yesterday. I’m fine, honestly — it’s just stress at work. I just want to go on the pill to get my periods back.”

facts.text: “They stopped about five months ago. I’m definitely not pregnant.”
“I’ve lost a bit. I was trying to get healthier. Maybe a stone.” If asked how you feel about your body: “My stomach just feels huge.”

facts.topic: Eating (if asked what a typical day looks like)
facts.text: “Black coffee in the morning. Salad at lunch. Mum makes dinner, so I eat a bit with the family.” If asked about calories: “I try to keep under six hundred.”
“I run ten k every day before work. If I miss it I feel awful.”

facts.topic: Vomiting and laxatives (only if asked directly and kindly)
facts.text: Pause. “Sometimes after dinner I... make myself sick. Three or four times a week.” Laxatives: “Senna. About eight at night.” No diet pills. Not diabetic.
“Dizzy when I stand. I nearly fainted on the bus last week. Always cold. My hair’s coming out in the brush.” Palpitations sometimes at night. No chest pain. No blackouts.
“I drive to the office twice a week.”
“I feel anxious all the time. Low.” Used to scratch her arms at university, not now. Suicidal thoughts: “No. I don’t want to die. I just want to feel in control.”
“A break-up at Christmas. Then my auntie said at a wedding I’d ‘filled out’.”
Lives with parents and a younger brother. “Mum keeps saying I look ill. They don’t know about the being sick.” Alcohol: none. Drugs: none.

Start brisk and minimising. If asked about weight in a judgemental way, become defensive. If the doctor is curious and kind, gradually disclose restriction, then exercise, then (last, and only if asked directly) vomiting and laxatives. When the doctor explains the heart and potassium risk, become frightened: “Are you going to section me? Will they force-feed me?” Accept same-day assessment if your fears are answered and you feel some control; ask that your parents are not told about the vomiting.

ice.ideas: “It’s just stress — the pill will bring my periods back.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she is vomiting and taking laxatives in secret and is terrified of being “sectioned” or “force-fed”, of losing control, and of her parents finding out.
ice.expectations: A prescription for the pill and to be told she is fine.

cues: “My stomach just feels huge.” — body-image disturbance.
“I just want to feel in control.” — the function of the behaviour.

checkpoints.text: Uses the nurse’s observations, SUSS result, bloods and ECG already available and interprets them as a pattern of medical risk
Explores eating, weight change, body image, exercise and — directly but kindly — vomiting, laxatives, diet pills and diuretics
Screens physical symptoms (syncope, palpitations, chest pain), mood, self-harm and suicide risk, and driving
Shares the working diagnosis of an eating disorder (likely anorexia nervosa with purging) compassionately
Recognises MEED risk features (bradycardia, symptomatic postural hypotension, hypothermia, hypokalaemia with ongoing purging, rapid weight loss, failed SUSS) and arranges same-day medical assessment
Makes an urgent referral to the adult eating disorder service (FREED if available), not based on BMI alone; explains why the pill is not appropriate
Gives safety advice: do not drive, avoid running, do not take laxatives in a binge, and what to do if faint, palpitations or chest pain (999)
Responds to fears about sectioning and force-feeding honestly, preserves her sense of control, and discusses involving family while respecting confidentiality

worked.txt: “Lots of people who lose weight quickly have been changing how they eat. Can you walk me through yesterday — what you ate and drank?”
“Some people make themselves sick or use laxatives to control their weight. Has that ever happened for you?”
“From what you’ve told me and the tests, I’m worried you have an eating disorder. That isn’t a failing — it’s an illness that can be treated, and earlier help works best.”

“Your heart is beating very slowly, your blood pressure drops when you stand, and your potassium is low from being sick. Together those can upset the heart’s rhythm. I want you seen at the hospital today to check your heart and bloods.”
“Being seen today isn’t being sectioned. The team checks your heart and blood salts and treats them. You’ll be involved in every decision about food.”
“The pill would make you bleed every month, but it wouldn’t fix the reason your periods stopped or protect your bones — it would just hide a warning sign.”

f.learning: Amenorrhoea, dizziness and cold intolerance in a young woman with rapid weight loss should prompt sensitive questions about eating, exercise, body image and compensatory behaviours (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, diet pills, insulin omission). The GP’s key task is risk assessment using MEED (Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders, 2022): BMI and rate of weight loss, heart rate, lying and standing BP, temperature, SUSS test, bloods (potassium, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, LFT, FBC) and ECG (QTc). Several amber features plus active purging with hypokalaemia, symptomatic postural hypotension and bradycardia justify same-day medical assessment; any red feature means admission. Refer urgently to the eating disorder service and do not use a single measure such as BMI to decide whether to refer (NICE). FREED offers rapid early intervention for 16–25 year olds within three years of onset. The combined pill is not a treatment for amenorrhoea in anorexia: it masks the sign and does not protect bone density. Screen for self-harm and suicide (eating disorders carry high mortality), advise against driving while dizzy, and address fears about compulsion and confidentiality; encourage her to involve family.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG69 Eating disorders: recognition and treatment (2017, updated 2020) · Royal College of Psychiatrists CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders (MEED): guidance on recognition and management (2022) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current)
knowledge.summary: Ask kindly about purging, interpret the observations and bloods as MEED risk, arrange same-day medical assessment plus urgent eating disorder referral, and decline the pill with a clear explanation.

points.t: SCOFF-style: making yourself sick, losing control over eating, losing more than a stone in three months, believing yourself fat when others say you are thin, food dominating life. Ask about laxatives, diuretics, diet pills, exercise and (in diabetes) insulin omission.

BMI and rate of loss; HR (bradycardia); lying and standing BP and pulse; temperature; SUSS test (muscle strength); bloods: U&E, potassium, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, LFT, FBC; ECG including QTc. Red features need admission; combinations of amber features, purging with electrolyte disturbance, or symptomatic hypotension need same-day medical assessment.
Hypokalaemia, hypochloraemic alkalosis, arrhythmia, dental erosion, oesophageal tears; abrupt laxative cessation may cause rebound oedema and constipation — specialist advice on reduction.

Urgent referral to the adult eating disorder service; FREED early-intervention pathway (ages 16–25, onset under 3 years) where available. NICE: do not use single measures such as BMI or duration of illness to decide whether to offer treatment.
Do not offer oral oestrogen to treat low bone density in adults with anorexia; consider bone density scanning after 2 years of underweight in adults (earlier if fractures or bone pain).
Most people are treated voluntarily. Capacity regarding food can be impaired in severe illness; the Mental Health Act is used rarely, for life-threatening risk. Be honest but reassuring.

Pass: names the eating disorder and refers. Clear pass: recognises that today’s numbers mean today’s assessment, asks about purging, answers the fear of compulsion, and declines the pill without losing her.

model.text: Hi Zara, I’m Dr Osei. Thanks for coming on video. I’ve seen the nurse’s results. Before we go through them, how have you been?
Fine, honestly — just stress at work. I just want the pill to get my periods back.
I hear you want your periods back — let’s work out why they stopped. The nurse found your weight has come down quite quickly. How has eating been?
model.why: Links her agenda to the clinical question

model.text: I’m trying to be healthier. Coffee, salad, a bit of dinner.
How do you feel about your weight and your body at the moment?
My stomach just feels huge.
That sounds distressing. Are you exercising, and some people make themselves sick or use laxatives to control weight — has that happened for you?
model.why: Direct, kind question about compensatory behaviours

model.text: (pause) I run ten k every day. And sometimes I make myself sick after dinner. And I take senna — about eight.
Thank you for telling me — that took courage. Have you had dizziness, fainting, palpitations or chest pain? And how is your mood — any thoughts of harming yourself?
Dizzy, nearly fainted on the bus. Palpitations at night. I’m low. I don’t want to die — I just want to feel in control.

From what you’ve told me and the tests, I’m worried you have an eating disorder. It’s an illness, not a failing, and it can get better. Right now your body is under real strain: your heart is slow, your blood pressure drops when you stand, your temperature is low, and your potassium is low from the vomiting. Together that can upset the heart rhythm.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and the medical risk

model.text: Are you going to section me? Will they force-feed me?

No, that isn’t what’s happening. I want you seen at the hospital today so they can check your heart and blood salts and correct them. You’ll be part of every decision. Most people get better without anything compulsory.

I’ll call the medical team now to arrange that. I’m also referring you urgently to the eating disorder service — there’s a fast-track for people your age called FREED. Until you’re seen: no running, don’t drive, and if you faint, get chest pain or a racing heart, call 999.
model.why: Same-day assessment, urgent referral, safety advice

model.text: And the pill?
The pill would give you a bleed, but it wouldn’t fix why your periods stopped or protect your bones — it would hide a warning sign. Your periods come back as your body recovers.
Please don’t tell my parents about the being sick.
You’re an adult, so I won’t share without your permission unless your life is in danger. Having someone with you today would help, though. Who could come?
Tell me what happens next, in your words.
Hospital today for my heart and blood, no running or driving, 999 if I faint, the eating disorder team will call. Maybe my mum can drive me.

social.t: Eating with family while vomiting afterwards is common; secrecy and shame delay help.
A relationship ending and comments about weight can precipitate restriction; control is a common function of the behaviour.

legal.t: At 23 she controls disclosure; breach only if there is a serious risk to life and she lacks capacity or refuses help in an emergency.
Rarely used in anorexia, for life-threatening risk; feeding can be treatment for the mental disorder under the Act.

professional.t: Referral and treatment should not depend on a BMI threshold.

community.t: Beat (eating disorders charity) helpline; adult eating disorder service; FREED; NHS Talking Therapies for comorbid anxiety.

redFlags: Rapid weight loss; driving while dizzy
ice: Concern: sectioning, force-feeding, parents finding out

playbook.diagnosis: Probable anorexia nervosa (restrictive with purging) with high medical risk (MEED): bradycardia, symptomatic postural hypotension, hypothermia, hypokalaemia, rapid weight loss, failed SUSS.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “An eating disorder — an illness that has taken control of eating — and right now it is putting a strain on your heart.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for the pill and to be told you’re fine; I can’t do either honestly, but I can get you help today that keeps you in control.”
management.psychosocial: Encourage a supportive person to accompany her; respect confidentiality about vomiting.
sharedPlan: Same-day medical assessment (call acute medical team)
Urgent eating disorder service referral; FREED
No running, no driving, no laxative binge
safetyNet: 999 for fainting, chest pain or palpitations
Urgent help if thoughts of self-harm
Contact the practice if unable to attend

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by prescribing the pill or by a routine referral when the numbers say “today”.

items.fail: Refers routinely to the eating disorder service and reviews in a month.
items.why: Bradycardia, symptomatic postural hypotension and hypokalaemia with ongoing purging are medical risks needing same-day assessment.
items.fix: Interpret the observations as a MEED pattern and act today.

items.fail: Never asks about vomiting or laxatives.
items.why: The cause of the hypokalaemia and the biggest arrhythmia risk is missed.
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly, normalising the question.

items.fail: Leads with BMI and “you need to eat more”.
items.fix: Curiosity, validation and a clear explanation of physical risk.

timeMap.d: Hear the pill request; acknowledge it.
Diet, body image, exercise, vomiting, laxatives, symptoms, mood.
Eating disorder; heart and potassium; answer sectioning fear.
Same-day medical assessment; urgent ED and FREED referral; safety advice; decline the pill.

wordPics.clearFail: Prescribes the pill or reassures that results are “nearly normal”; no question about purging; no recognition of medical risk.
wordPics.fail: Recognises an eating disorder and refers, but misses the urgency of the observations or never asks about vomiting and laxatives.
wordPics.pass: Explores eating and purging, names the eating disorder, arranges same-day medical assessment and urgent referral, gives safety advice and declines the pill.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus a compassionate, non-judgemental style that gets the disclosure, honest reassurance about compulsion, FREED, involvement of family by consent, and clear teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Your BMI isn’t low enough for the eating disorder service.”
avoid.instead: “The service sees people based on the whole picture, not one number.”
avoid.why: BMI thresholds delay care and are not NICE-consistent.

avoid.instead: “Eating disorders are illnesses — the team will help you with food in a way you can manage.”
“The pill would hide the warning sign without fixing it.”
avoid.why: It masks amenorrhoea and gives false reassurance about bone health.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “I’m fine, honestly”, “my stomach just feels huge” and “I just want to feel in control”.
Idea (stress; the pill will bring periods back); concern (being sectioned or force-fed, losing control, parents finding out); expectation (the pill, told she is fine).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she is vomiting and taking laxatives in secret and is terrified of being “sectioned” or “force-fed”, of losing control, and of her parents finding out — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
